title: This post is only for Beginner Game Devs, Not pros
author: shottycoin
selftext:
Hey everybody! Have a question for ya. After discovering a tool, does not matter, if its AI image, audio or code, text and etc. what is the most important thing for you on that tool. Easy to use user interface but limited functionality or the tool with some learning curve but with advanced features.

Just to compare: look at Canva, and Photoshop. One is for amateurs, non designers, looking to get quick design jobs done. Photoshop is for people, who are trying to get the job done with more advanced features. probably with photoshop you will get better results (if you know how to use it), with Canva you will be the fastest. Which one you prefer most? Thanks in advance.

comments.author: Opening-West-4369
comments.body: ai tools don't really work like that, just depends on model & prompt

replies.author: GaiusVictor
replies.body: If this was true, tools like ComfyUI wouldn't exist.

replies.author: shottycoin
replies.body: AI tools is not LLM actually. AI Tools offering user interface powered by AI.

comments.author: Leather_Tomorrow4993
comments.body: for me the its the speed. Im new to gamedev. can spend max 2 hrs per week on that. Whenever I use any platform, just checking if I can do something with less amount of time. By profession im designer. I hated canva for a long time, but now sometimes im also using it just to avoid unnecessary work burden with photoshop.

comments.author: agarlington
comments.body:
knowing what model I'm working with, to properly get it into my workflow and know token usage etc.. I need to know if I'm coding with grok vs claude  sonnet lol.

 so In short UI/UX guess?

comments.author: MysteriousPepper8908
comments.body: I just don't think you have to choose with most tools. Blender and Photoshop are both powerful tools which are also rather intuitive. I think the next level where you can start to debate whether it's truly needed is when you get to specialist tools like Zbrush and Substance Painter which can really accelerate your process if you know how to use them but many people get by without. Choosing an engine is more tricky. I find Unity to be fairly accessible but still powerful while Unreal feels more unapproachable but maybe that's just what I'm familiar with. If you're making something not too graphically demanding, something like Godot might be a more accessible option.

replies.author: Gothmagog
replies.body: I think calling Blender intuitive is... misleading.

replies.author: MysteriousPepper8908
replies.body: I guess it's all relative but I don't think it's bad relative to other similarly advanced 3D modeling programs and it's way better than it was 5-10 years ago.

comments.author: DoubleDeann
comments.body: From my experience. A better tool with more advanced features. Taking the time to learn a tool has always paid off, and I feel like all of the fast workarounds I tried just didn't give the results I wanted. If your expectations are low, maybe easy/fast is okay. It really depends on the tool as well. Some are better than others naturally.

comments.author: Gothmagog
comments.body: I'm new to game dev, but am an old tech guy, so I grok software pretty easily and therefore go for 1/something free/opensource, and 2/something that will actually achieve the results I need. This usually leads me to look at deep, well-established opensource tools.

comments.author: ineedthealgorithm
comments.body: I prefer the tool that has no or a minimal learning curve. It shouldn't be cluttered with so many functionalities. Just ones that really solve a problem for users are enough.

comments.author: melonboy55
comments.body:
I suspect that people overestimate how complicated the software should be

It's not that people can't understand complicated software, I just think they won't try unless very motivated.

I worked pretty hard to get my tool *simple* and had friends and family play test it - but actual users still make tons of mistakes - every mistake is painful and they aren't likely to give it a second try.

I want my tool to give people a lot of raw power, and to do that I need to expose some complicated things. 

I'm trying to find a way to make it look simple from the outside, but as you dive deeper you realize how powerful it can be. - I think a lot of games do this really well. The Factorio tutorial for example
